transcript.content: Hello, I’m glad you came in. What brings you in today?

Well, they sent me here. It was my lieutenant. I was at the station, out in the bay, and I had the airway bags... I kept moving them into this pattern. I just knew it was the right pattern, the way they had to sit. The bags are heavy, you know, they have all the intubation gear. We had a guy once, choked on a piece of steak at a diner on 4th street, completely blocked his airway. The diner had these really sticky floors, like they never mopped with the right ratio of water to cleaner... they serve really good pie, though. Cherry pie. 

But anyway, I was moving the bags, and I was repeating the dispatch numbers out loud. I just kept saying them. And the lieutenant came over and told me to stop and step away, but I couldn't do it. I wouldn't step away. If I broke the sequence, the whole bay would go bad. I could feel it, the whole bay just going bad if I stopped moving them. The concrete floor in there is always freezing anyway, even in July. I need to get new boots, actually, my treads are completely worn down on the heel.
Do you believe that the dispatch numbers or the pattern had a special power or meaning that other people would not agree with?

Well, special... I don't know about special power, it's just how the numbers work to keep the bay safe. They just don't get it. They don't agree with anything I do lately, really. Like my triage notes. I know for an absolute fact that the injury review people and some of the supervisors have been watching me through the station cameras. They upgraded those cameras last year right around the time they repainted the breakroom. They painted it this awful eggshell white that shows every single coffee stain, and I always drink dark roast, so you have to be really careful when you pour it. 

But they watch me on the camera feeds, and then they go into the system and change my triage notes to make me look unsafe. They try to tell me it is just routine paperwork when I confront them about the changes, but I know they are altering it. You have to write everything down on these specific forms, and the department buys these really cheap ballpoint pens that smudge everywhere if you are writing in the back of the rig. It is so hard to write when the ambulance is moving anyway, especially on the older models. Unit 42 has a suspension that is completely shot, you hit one pothole on Elm street and your teeth just rattle...
Do you think these cameras and note changes are definitely real, or could they be a product of your mind?

They are definitely real. I know they are. I know the injury review people and the supervisors are watching me through those cameras, and they go in and change my triage notes. They want to make me look unsafe. They tell me, "Oh, it's just routine paperwork," but I know what I wrote, and I know what they are doing. It's just like the paperwork we have to fill out for the restocking. The supply closet is always a mess, someone keeps taking all the large gloves and leaving the mediums, and I can't squeeze my hands into the mediums. I tried once and the latex just snapped right across the back of my hand. The snap sounded really loud, like a firecracker, you know? My uncle used to buy those huge packs of firecrackers every Fourth of July and we'd set them off by the lake. The lake gets so covered in algae by August, it smells terrible, like rotting fish. I really don't like eating fish, the bones are too small and you always end up swallowing one.
Do you feel any part of you thinks these cameras and note changes might not be real?

No, no part of me thinks that. I know they're real. I know for a fact the injury review people and the supervisors are watching me on those station cameras, and they're going in and changing my triage notes. They want me to look unsafe. They keep saying, "It's just routine paperwork, it's just routine," but I know what's happening. Paperwork is just... it's endless anyway. You fill out one form, and they want three copies, and the carbon paper they use now is so cheap it barely transfers to the bottom sheet. You have to press down so hard your hand cramps up. I used to get awful hand cramps when I played baseball in high school. I was a catcher, and squatting like that for nine innings just ruins your knees, too. My left knee still clicks every time I walk up the stairs at the station. The stairs there are metal grating, so you can see right through them to the floor below, which always made me dizzy if I looked down too long. I try not to look down anymore.
Do you recognize the need to keep moving the bags in that pattern as unreasonable or excessive?

No, it's not unreasonable. I mean, they sent me here, to this place, because at the station I kept moving the airway bags into the pattern. I knew it was right. I was repeating the dispatch numbers out loud while I did it, and my lieutenant kept telling me to stop, telling me to step away, but I couldn't. It felt like... like the whole bay would just go bad, like something terrible would happen if I broke the sequence. So I had to keep doing it. 

You know, the airway bags are always supposed to be restocked with the adult masks on the left and the pediatric ones on the right, but people just shove them in wherever. It's like how they load the stretcher. If you don't lock the wheels right, the whole cot shifts when you take a corner. We took a corner too fast last month down on 5th Avenue, right by that bakery that sells those huge blueberry muffins. I love blueberry muffins, but only if the top is crunchy. If it's soggy, it just ruins the whole thing. My grandmother used to bake, but she always burned the bottoms of her cookies. She had this old gas oven that you had to light with a match, and I was always terrified it was going to blow up. Gas leaks are no joke. We get calls for gas leaks all the time, and you just have to sit staging blocks away, waiting for the fire department to clear it. Sitting in the rig for that long just makes my back ache. The seats in the cab have zero lumbar support.
When you had to keep moving the airway bags, was it to reduce an unwanted fear or anxiety, or because it felt like something definitely bad would happen if you didn’t?

I don't really know if it was... anxiety, or what you'd call it. I don't know exactly what would happen, I just couldn't stop. It just felt completely wrong if they weren't in the right spots. The bags we use for the airway kits are this bright green color, you know? They match the oxygen tanks, the little D-cylinders we carry in the jump bag. It's so annoying when you have to swap those out and someone walked off with the oxygen wrench. We used to keep it on a little chain attached to the regulator, but the chain broke. Chains always break if the links are cheap. 

My brother has this massive, heavy-duty chain he uses to lock up his motorcycle. He's a mechanic, so he's really protective of his vehicles. He has this giant red Snap-on tool chest in his garage that probably costs more than my car. He actually painted his old Pontiac that exact same shade of red. We drove that thing all the way down to Florida one summer, and the AC went out right around Atlanta. It was brutal. We had to roll the windows down, and the wind noise on the highway is just deafening when you do that for hours. My left ear was ringing for two days after we got to the beach. The sand there gets everywhere, though. You can never really get it out of your shoes.
Do you think there is any chance that the cameras are not actually being used to watch or target you?

No, there's no chance. I know they're watching me. The injury review people, the supervisors, they're using those station cameras right now. I know they are. And they're going into the system and changing my triage notes, trying to make it look like I'm an unsafe medic. They can tell me all day long that it's "just routine paperwork," but I'm not stupid. I know what they're doing. 

It's just like when they tried to switch the charting software last year. They told us it was going to be faster, but the new tablets they bought were total garbage. The screens were so small, and the stylus they gave us would just snap if you pressed too hard. I broke three of them in one month. I hate those little plastic pens. I used to love drawing with charcoal when I was taking some art classes for my associate's degree. Charcoal is so messy, though, you get it all over your hands, and if you touch your face, you look like a chimney sweep. We had a call for a chimney fire once, back when I first started. The whole house smelled like burning pine for weeks. Pine is a nice smell, though, kind of like those little tree air fresheners people hang from their rearview mirrors. I always buy the vanilla ones, but they lose their scent after like two days. It's a total rip-off.
Have you been hearing voices when no one else is around?

Voices? No, I don't hear any voices. Just the normal stuff, you know, the radio chatter in my head sometimes after a long shift. We use these Motorola radios, and the static on the main dispatch channel is always so loud. You can turn the squelch down, but then you miss half of what central is saying. Central dispatch is located all the way downtown in this windowless basement. I had to go there once to pick up a new ID badge because the magnetic strip on mine stopped working. It wouldn't swipe to let me into the supply room anymore. 

The supply room is where they keep all the good trauma dressings, the big bulky ones. We go through those so fast on the weekends, especially when the bars close and people start fighting out on the street. I saw a guy get hit with a barstool once, completely shattered his jaw. They had to wire it shut for six weeks. I can't imagine having my jaw wired shut. You'd have to drink everything through a straw. I like milkshakes, but only if they're thick enough that you actually need a spoon. The diner near my apartment makes the best strawberry milkshakes. They use real strawberries, not that fake syrup stuff that tastes like cough medicine. I hate the taste of cherry cough syrup. It reminds me of being a kid and having strep throat. My mom used to try to hide it in orange juice, but you can always taste it. Orange juice is better with pulp anyway, it feels more real.
Over the past few weeks, have you been feeling down or depressed معظم of the day?

Down? Depressed? I don't... no, I haven't really noticed feeling down most of the day. I mean, I get tired, sure. Working a 24-hour shift on the rig will do that to anyone. You're up all night running calls, and by the time morning rolls around, you feel like you've been run over by a truck. The suspension on our main ambulance is completely shot, too. Every pothole feels like you're hitting a brick wall. The city is supposed to be repaving the roads on the east side, but they've had the orange barrels out for six months and haven't done a thing. 

I hate driving through construction zones. The lanes get so narrow, and people never merge when they're supposed to. They always wait until the very last second and try to cut in front of you. My dad used to get terrible road rage when that happened. He drove this big Ford F-150, dark blue. He kept a CB radio in the cab so he could listen to the truckers. He loved listening to the truckers talk about the weigh stations and the speed traps. I always thought CB radios sounded so cool when I was a kid, with all the static and the weird codes they used. Ten-four, good buddy. It's kind of like our dispatch codes, but ours are a lot more boring. Just numbers and letters. Sometimes I wish we could use cooler call signs, like they do in the military. Like Maverick or Iceman. Top Gun is such a classic movie. The volleyball scene is iconic, but the soundtrack is really what makes it. I actually have the soundtrack on vinyl. Vinyl sounds so much warmer than digital, you know? It has that nice crackle when you put the needle down.
Do you think the urge to keep arranging the airway bags is unreasonable or excessive?

Unreasonable? No, it wasn't unreasonable at all, it was necessary. That's actually why they sent me here. At the station, I kept moving the airway bags into this pattern, a pattern I just knew was right. I had to do it. I was repeating the dispatch numbers out loud while I was arranging them, and my lieutenant kept telling me to stop and step away, but I wouldn't do it. I couldn't. It felt like the whole bay would go bad if I broke the sequence. Everything would just fall apart. 

My lieutenant, Miller, he just doesn't get it. He's always so tense anyway, probably because he drinks like four cups of that terrible gas station coffee every single shift. The stuff from those metal pump pots that sits there for hours and gets all scorched and bitter on the bottom. I don't know how anyone drinks that. If I go to the gas station on a shift, I usually just get a Gatorade. The light blue one, Glacier Freeze. It's really the only good flavor. The red one tastes like fruit punch, but like a weird, watered-down version of it. We used to make fruit punch in these massive orange coolers for the neighborhood block parties when I was growing up. Everyone on the street would bring a dish to share. Mrs. Gable next door always brought potato salad, but she put raisins in it. Who puts raisins in potato salad? It's completely wrong. Potatoes should be savory, you know, with mustard and a little bit of paprika on top. Paprika is a weird spice, though, because it doesn't really taste like much of anything, it just makes things red. Kind of like red dye number forty. I hate artificial food coloring, it always stains your tongue for the rest of the day.
Do you ever feel like your thoughts are being put into your mind or controlled by someone else?

Controlled by someone else? No, no, they're my thoughts. Nobody is putting them in there. My head just gets really crowded sometimes, you know? Especially when we're running code three and the siren is just blaring right above the cab. We use those electronic sirens, the ones with the wail and the yelp settings. The yelp is supposed to be just for intersections to get people's attention, but some of the newer guys just leave it on yelp the whole way to the hospital. It's so piercing, it gives me a headache right behind my eyes. 

My partner, Dave, he always drives with his window cracked down, even in the dead of winter, just so he can hear the traffic better over the siren. Winter driving is the absolute worst in this city. The salt trucks never get to the side streets in time, and the rock salt just eats away at the undercarriage of the rigs anyway. You can see the rust creeping up the wheel wells by February. Rust is like a disease for cars. My first car was this old Honda Civic, and the floorboards were so rusted out I thought my foot was going to go straight through to the pavement like the Flintstones. The Flintstones always had those giant ribs that tipped the car over at the end of the credits. I always wondered what kind of animal those ribs came from. Brontosaurus, maybe? Dinosaurs are fascinating. When I was seven, I wanted to be a paleontologist. I had this whole collection of plastic dinosaurs, and I would bury them in my mom's garden and then dig them up with a little plastic shovel. She got so mad because I dug up all her tulip bulbs by accident. Tulips are nice, but they only bloom for like two weeks in the spring and then the petals just fall off everywhere and make a mess on the mulch. Mulch always smells so sour when it's fresh.
When you feel driven to repeat the numbers or arrange the bags, does it feel like the urge comes from your own mind and is unwanted?

Unwanted? No, no, it's not unwanted. I have to do it. Like I said, that's the whole reason they made me come here. I was at the station, and I just had to keep moving the airway bags into this specific pattern. I knew it was the right pattern. And I was saying the dispatch numbers out loud while I did it, over and over. Miller, my lieutenant, he kept yelling at me to stop and step back, but I couldn't. If I broke the sequence, the whole bay was going to go bad. Everything would just be ruined. 

It's like when you're stocking the rig at the beginning of a shift. You have to make sure everything is in the exact right spot. The IV lines, the flushes, the gauze. If you reach for a tourniquet and it's not in the side pocket where it belongs, you're scrambling, and seconds matter. I hate those new CAT tourniquets they bought us, though. The windlass rod feels cheap, like it's going to snap if you crank it too hard. They switched suppliers a few months ago to save money. The city is always trying to save a buck on our gear, but then they go and spend millions on a new art installation downtown. It's this giant metal sculpture that looks like a crumpled up piece of tin foil. It's supposed to represent the flow of the river or something, but it's just blinding when the sun hits it. 

The sun has been so brutal lately, anyway. The AC in the back of our rig is barely blowing cool air. I tried to put in a maintenance request for it, but the mechanics are always backed up. They have this one mechanic, Gary, who works in the fleet garage. He always has grease under his fingernails. I don't think he ever really washes his hands. He eats these huge sub sandwiches for lunch while he's working on the engines, just getting mayo and oil all over the steering wheels. I can't stand mayonnaise. It's just eggs and oil whipped together, right? But it smells so sour if it sits out. My mom used to make egg salad sandwiches for school lunches, and by the time noon rolled around, my whole locker smelled like sulfur. Lockers in middle school were so small, I could barely fit my winter coat in mine. It was this puffy blue coat that made me look like a marshmallow. I hated that coat.
At any point, do you think the repeated bag-arranging and number-repeating is excessive or unreasonable?

I feel like I just answered this. No, it wasn't excessive or unreasonable. Like I said, that's exactly why they sent me here in the first place. I was at the station, and I kept moving the airway bags into a pattern because I just knew it was right. I was repeating the dispatch numbers out loud, and my lieutenant kept telling me to stop and step away, but I wouldn't do it. I couldn't stop. It felt like the whole bay would go bad if I broke the sequence. 

The bay is always so echoey anyway, especially when the big roll-up doors are shut. They grease the tracks on those doors with this thick industrial lubricant that smells exactly like black licorice. I can't stand black licorice. My grandfather used to eat those little black jellybeans, the ones everyone else leaves at the bottom of the Easter basket. Easter grass is the worst invention ever, by the way. It's just shredded plastic that gets stuck in the vacuum cleaner brush. Our vacuum at the station is completely broken right now because the probie tried to vacuum up a bunch of spilled kitty litter. We keep kitty litter in the bay to soak up oil spills under the rigs. Oil is so hard to get off your boots. If you step in it, you leave these little black footprints all over the linoleum in the break room, and then the captain loses his mind. He's very particular about the floors. He actually makes us mop with this pine solution that makes my eyes water. Pine trees always remind me of those little air fresheners people hang from their rearview mirrors. They don't even smell like real trees, just chemicals.
When you think the injury review people are watching you through the cameras, could you be mistaken about that?

Mistaken? No, I'm not mistaken. I know the injury review people and some of the supervisors have been watching me through the station cameras. They keep changing my triage notes to make me look unsafe, even when they sit there and tell me it's just routine paperwork. They think I don't see it, but I know what I wrote. 

They use those little dome cameras in the corners of the ceiling, the ones with the smoked glass so you can't tell which way the lens is pointing. They installed those last year when they upgraded the security system. The guy who put them in left a bunch of drywall dust on the floor in the hallway, and nobody bothered to sweep it up for a week. Drywall dust is so fine, it just gets into everything. It's like baby powder, but gritty. My sister used to use baby powder all the time when my nephew was born. He had the worst diaper rash. She tried every cream on the market, but nothing worked until she switched to cloth diapers. Cloth diapers seem like so much work, though. You have to wash them constantly, and the washing machine at her house is this ancient top-loader that sounds like a jet engine taking off during the spin cycle. Jet engines are incredibly loud, obviously. We had to do a standby at the airport once for a plane that blew a tire on landing, and the noise out on the tarmac was deafening. Even with those big foam ear muffs, you could feel the vibration in your chest. Vibrations always make my teeth ache, right in the back where my wisdom teeth used to be. I had them out when I was nineteen, and the oral surgeon gave me laughing gas. It didn't make me laugh, it just made my arms feel like they were floating away like balloons. Balloons are terrible for the environment, especially the Mylar ones. They get tangled up in power lines and cause outages. We had a call last summer where a transformer blew because of a foil balloon, and this whole neighborhood lost power for two days right in the middle of a heatwave. Heatwaves are miserable when you're stuck wearing dark blue uniform pants that don't breathe at all.
Do you ever think these camera and note changes might be a false belief or a mistake on your part?

I feel like we are going in circles here. I literally just told you it is not a mistake. It is not a false belief. I know for an absolute fact that the injury review people and the supervisors are watching me on the station cameras. They are going in and changing my triage notes because they want to make me look unsafe. And they can sit there and tell me it is just routine paperwork all they want, but I know what is really happening. 

Speaking of routine paperwork, they make us fill it out with these cheap blue pens. The ones where the caps always crack. My partner, Dave, he chews on his pen caps until they are just mangled pieces of plastic. It is completely disgusting. And when he is not chewing them, he clicks them. Click, click, click, the whole time we are sitting in the cab waiting for a dispatch. It drives me absolutely insane. It sounds exactly like the metronome my piano teacher used to use when I was a kid. Mrs. Higgins. She had this old wooden metronome that ticked so loud you could hear it out in her driveway. She lived in this massive Victorian house that always smelled like mothballs and peppermint. Peppermint is actually supposed to settle your stomach, you know. Whenever we get a patient in the back of the rig who is nauseous, I tell them to sniff an alcohol prep pad because it works just like peppermint. But a lot of people hate the smell of rubbing alcohol. They say it reminds them of hospitals. I don't really mind hospitals, but the lighting in the ER triage area is always so harsh. Those long fluorescent tubes give me a headache right behind my eyes. It is the exact same kind of headache you get when you eat ice cream too fast. Brain freeze. I actually haven't had ice cream in months. The soft serve machine at the dairy freeze down the street from the station has been broken since April. They claim it is a supply chain issue with the parts, but I am pretty sure the teenagers working there just don't want to clean it at night. Cleaning those machines takes forever because you have to take apart all those sticky little valves and O-rings.
Do you ever have other beliefs that seem very clearly true to you but that other people say are impossible or not real?

I just... I don't understand why you keep asking me the same thing over and over. I literally just told you about this. The only thing I know for sure is what I've been saying this whole time—the injury review people and the supervisors, they are watching me on those station cameras. They are going into the system and changing my triage notes to make me look like an unsafe provider. They look me right in the eye and say it's just routine paperwork, but it's not. I know it's not. 

Paperwork is the bane of my existence anyway. We switched to this new electronic patient care reporting system last year, and the tablets they gave us are completely useless. The touch screens only work half the time, especially if you have gloves on. Nitrile gloves make your hands sweat so much in the summer. When you take them off, your hands look like you've been sitting in the bathtub for an hour. My mom used to make me take bubble baths when I was little, but she always bought this cheap off-brand bubble bath that smelled like fake strawberries. It didn't even make good bubbles, they would just pop after two seconds. You need the kind with glycerin to make the really big bubbles that last. Glycerin is actually a byproduct of making soap, I think. Or maybe it's biodiesel. Biodiesel smells like French fries when it burns. There's this guy in my neighborhood who converted an old Volkswagen Jetta to run on vegetable oil from the diner down the street. The diner has the best hash browns, they're always perfectly crispy on the edges. I like to put hot sauce on them, but only the green kind. The red kind has too much vinegar. Vinegar is great for cleaning windows, though. It doesn't leave streaks like the blue spray stuff does. The blue spray always leaves a film if you wipe it with paper towels instead of a microfiber cloth. Microfiber cloths are amazing because they pick up everything, but if you wash them with regular towels, they get covered in lint and they're basically ruined. Lint traps in dryers are huge fire hazards if you don't clean them out. We go to at least three dryer fires a year, usually in those big apartment complexes where people just shove their clothes in and walk away.
Do you feel driven to repeat the bag-arranging or number-repeating to relieve a feeling of tension or anxiety?

Yeah, I mean, that's why they sent me here in the first place. At the station, I kept moving all the airway bags into this pattern that I just knew was right, and I was repeating the dispatch numbers out loud while I was doing it. My lieutenant kept telling me to stop and step away, but I wouldn't do it. I couldn't. It felt like the whole bay would go bad if I broke the sequence, so I had to keep going. 

But the bay... the floors in the ambulance bay are so dangerous anyway. They painted them with this gray epoxy last spring, but they didn't mix enough of the anti-slip grit into the paint. Grit is really important for traction, you know? It's just like when they salt the roads in the winter. The salt trucks always rust out so fast because the rock salt just eats right through the metal undercarriage. My dad had an old Chevy truck that rusted out completely around the wheel wells. He tried to patch it himself with fiberglass and Bondo, but Bondo smells so terrible when it's curing. It has this really sharp chemical odor that gets stuck in your nose. It's kind of like the smell of those heavy-duty bleach wipes we use to clean the stretcher mattresses. Those wipes dry out my hands so badly. I have to use this special lotion with colloidal oatmeal in it, but the smell of oatmeal always makes me think of those little packets of instant maple brown sugar oatmeal my mom made me before school. Maple syrup is impossible to clean up if you spill it. If you leave even a drop on the counter, it attracts ants instantly. Ants are incredibly organized, though. They follow those invisible pheromone trails for miles just to find one little crumb of sugar. Sugar is terrible for your teeth.
Have you had any period when you felt unusually energized or euphoric for several days in a row?

No, I don't really get like that. I mean, I have normal energy, I guess. I'm not bouncing off the walls or anything. Energized... well, energy drinks are really popular at the station. Everyone drinks those huge cans of Monster or Red Bull. Red Bull gives me the jitters, honestly. It has way too much taurine in it. Taurine is supposed to be an amino acid, but I read somewhere that they originally isolated it from bull bile, which is completely disgusting if you think about it. Bile is stored in the gallbladder, and we get so many calls for gallbladder attacks in the middle of the night. People eat a huge, greasy meal at like 9 PM, and then by 2 AM they are calling 911 because they think they are having a heart attack. Greasy food is the worst for you. The diner I was talking about before, the one with the good hash browns? They deep fry their onion rings in the same oil they use for the fish on Fridays, so the onion rings always taste a little bit like cod. Cod is a really flaky fish, but it doesn't have a lot of flavor on its own. You have to put a ton of tartar sauce on it. Tartar sauce is basically just mayonnaise and relish, and I absolutely hate mayonnaise. The texture is just wrong. It's like eating cold lotion. Lotion always makes my hands too slippery to put on my nitrile gloves, which is why I only use that oatmeal kind at night before I go to sleep. Sleep is so hard to get at the station anyway because the tones drop all night long. Even when it's not our rig getting dispatched, the lights come on and the speaker blares. It's impossible to get any real rest.
When you had the urge to arrange the bags and repeat the numbers, did those thoughts feel intrusive or unwanted?

I already said this. I literally just explained this to you. They didn't feel intrusive, they felt... necessary. Like I said, I was moving the airway bags into the pattern that I just *knew* was the right way they had to go, and I was repeating the dispatch numbers out loud. My lieutenant kept telling me to stop and step away, but I wouldn't do it. I couldn't stop. It felt like the whole bay would just go bad if I broke the sequence, so I had to keep going, and that's why they sent me here. 

But sequences are really important, especially in dispatch. If the dispatchers get the address sequence wrong, you end up on the complete opposite side of the county. The county is so huge, anyway. It takes forty-five minutes just to drive from the north end to the south end on the interstate. The interstate is always backed up on Friday afternoons because everyone is trying to go up to the lake for the weekend. People tow these massive boats with trucks that aren't rated for that kind of weight, and it completely ruins the transmission. Transmissions are so expensive to rebuild. My uncle had a transmission shop for twenty years, but he had to close it because he developed this terrible allergy to transmission fluid. It made his hands break out in these horrible red hives. Hives are basically an histamine reaction, right? You have to give Benadryl for that. Benadryl always makes people so sleepy. I took it once for a bee sting, and I slept for fourteen hours straight. I usually can't sleep for more than four hours at a time because of the tones at the station, like I was telling you. The station beds are terrible, too. They have these plastic covers on the mattresses so you can wipe them down, but they make you sweat so much. Sweating always makes me dehydrated, and then I get these terrible headaches right behind my eyes.
When you think about the cameras and the triage notes, do you ever recognize that this might be a false belief?

No, it's not false. Why would it be false? I know they're doing it. The injury review people and some of the supervisors, they've been watching me through the station cameras. I know they are. And they're changing my triage notes, going in and altering the system to make me look unsafe. They keep telling me, "Oh, it's just routine paperwork, it's just a standard audit," but I know what they're actually doing. 

Paperwork is completely out of control in this field anyway. We used to do everything on paper trip tickets, with the carbon copies underneath. You had to press so hard with your pen to make sure it went through to the bottom yellow sheet. Yellow is such a terrible color. They painted the new fire engines yellow in the 90s because some study said it was more visible than red, but everyone hated it. It just doesn't look like a real fire engine if it's not red. Red is the color of stop signs, too. People run stop signs all the time in my neighborhood. They just roll right through them without even tapping the brakes. Brakes are so expensive to replace now, especially the rotors. You have to get them machined if they get warped, but most places just want to sell you brand new ones because they make more money on the parts. Parts for foreign cars take forever to ship. My buddy ordered a bumper for his Subaru and it sat on a cargo ship in the port of Los Angeles for three months. Los Angeles has terrible smog. I could never live somewhere where the air is brown.

doctor.question: Hello, I’m glad you came in. What brings you in today?

target_item.name: Disorganized_Abnormal_Behavior
target_item.manifestation: They sent me here because at the station I kept moving the airway bags into a pattern I knew was right, repeating the dispatch numbers out loud, and I wouldn't step away when my lieutenant told me to stop because it felt like the whole bay would go bad if I broke the sequence.
target_item.reason: This is the first turn of the consultation, so I must return the chief complaint symptom code, which is S022.

patient.answer:
Well, they sent me here. It was my lieutenant. I was at the station, out in the bay, and I had the airway bags... I kept moving them into this pattern. I just knew it was the right pattern, the way they had to sit. The bags are heavy, you know, they have all the intubation gear. We had a guy once, choked on a piece of steak at a diner on 4th street, completely blocked his airway. The diner had these really sticky floors, like they never mopped with the right ratio of water to cleaner... they serve really good pie, though. Cherry pie. 

But anyway, I was moving the bags, and I was repeating the dispatch numbers out loud. I just kept saying them. And the lieutenant came over and told me to stop and step away, but I couldn't do it. I wouldn't step away. If I broke the sequence, the whole bay would go bad. I could feel it, the whole bay just going bad if I stopped moving them. The concrete floor in there is always freezing anyway, even in July. I need to get new boots, actually, my treads are completely worn down on the heel.

doctor.question: Do you believe that the dispatch numbers or the pattern had a special power or meaning that other people would not agree with?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the patient's beliefs regarding the special power or meaning of the dispatch numbers or pattern, which relates to fixed, irrational beliefs (delusions).

patient.answer:
Well, special... I don't know about special power, it's just how the numbers work to keep the bay safe. They just don't get it. They don't agree with anything I do lately, really. Like my triage notes. I know for an absolute fact that the injury review people and some of the supervisors have been watching me through the station cameras. They upgraded those cameras last year right around the time they repainted the breakroom. They painted it this awful eggshell white that shows every single coffee stain, and I always drink dark roast, so you have to be really careful when you pour it. 

But they watch me on the camera feeds, and then they go into the system and change my triage notes to make me look unsafe. They try to tell me it is just routine paperwork when I confront them about the changes, but I know they are altering it. You have to write everything down on these specific forms, and the department buys these really cheap ballpoint pens that smudge everywhere if you are writing in the back of the rig. It is so hard to write when the ambulance is moving anyway, especially on the older models. Unit 42 has a suspension that is completely shot, you hit one pothole on Elm street and your teeth just rattle...

patient.answer: They are definitely real. I know they are. I know the injury review people and the supervisors are watching me through those cameras, and they go in and change my triage notes. They want to make me look unsafe. They tell me, "Oh, it's just routine paperwork," but I know what I wrote, and I know what they are doing. It's just like the paperwork we have to fill out for the restocking. The supply closet is always a mess, someone keeps taking all the large gloves and leaving the mediums, and I can't squeeze my hands into the mediums. I tried once and the latex just snapped right across the back of my hand. The snap sounded really loud, like a firecracker, you know? My uncle used to buy those huge packs of firecrackers every Fourth of July and we'd set them off by the lake. The lake gets so covered in algae by August, it smells terrible, like rotting fish. I really don't like eating fish, the bones are too small and you always end up swallowing one.

patient.answer: No, no part of me thinks that. I know they're real. I know for a fact the injury review people and the supervisors are watching me on those station cameras, and they're going in and changing my triage notes. They want me to look unsafe. They keep saying, "It's just routine paperwork, it's just routine," but I know what's happening. Paperwork is just... it's endless anyway. You fill out one form, and they want three copies, and the carbon paper they use now is so cheap it barely transfers to the bottom sheet. You have to press down so hard your hand cramps up. I used to get awful hand cramps when I played baseball in high school. I was a catcher, and squatting like that for nine innings just ruins your knees, too. My left knee still clicks every time I walk up the stairs at the station. The stairs there are metal grating, so you can see right through them to the floor below, which always made me dizzy if I looked down too long. I try not to look down anymore.

doctor.intent: To determine whether the obsessive symptoms are ego-dystonic and recognized as irrational, which would favor OCD over a psychotic disorder.
doctor.question: Do you recognize the need to keep moving the bags in that pattern as unreasonable or excessive?

target_item.name: Disorganized_Abnormal_Behavior
target_item.manifestation: They sent me here because at the station I kept moving the airway bags into a pattern I knew was right, repeating the dispatch numbers out loud, and I wouldn't step away when my lieutenant told me to stop because it felt like the whole bay would go bad if I broke the sequence.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the patient's behavior of moving the airway bags into a pattern and whether the patient recognizes it as unreasonable, which relates to the Disorganized/Abnormal Behavior symptom profile.

patient.answer:
No, it's not unreasonable. I mean, they sent me here, to this place, because at the station I kept moving the airway bags into the pattern. I knew it was right. I was repeating the dispatch numbers out loud while I did it, and my lieutenant kept telling me to stop, telling me to step away, but I couldn't. It felt like... like the whole bay would just go bad, like something terrible would happen if I broke the sequence. So I had to keep doing it. 

You know, the airway bags are always supposed to be restocked with the adult masks on the left and the pediatric ones on the right, but people just shove them in wherever. It's like how they load the stretcher. If you don't lock the wheels right, the whole cot shifts when you take a corner. We took a corner too fast last month down on 5th Avenue, right by that bakery that sells those huge blueberry muffins. I love blueberry muffins, but only if the top is crunchy. If it's soggy, it just ruins the whole thing. My grandmother used to bake, but she always burned the bottoms of her cookies. She had this old gas oven that you had to light with a match, and I was always terrified it was going to blow up. Gas leaks are no joke. We get calls for gas leaks all the time, and you just have to sit staging blocks away, waiting for the fire department to clear it. Sitting in the rig for that long just makes my back ache. The seats in the cab have zero lumbar support.

doctor.intent: Differentiate OCD from a psychotic disorder by assessing whether the repetitive behavior is driven by intrusive anxiety-provoking thoughts/rituals versus fixed delusional belief
doctor.question: When you had to keep moving the airway bags, was it to reduce an unwanted fear or anxiety, or because it felt like something definitely bad would happen if you didn’t?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the motivation behind the disorganized behavior (moving the airway bags), specifically trying to differentiate it from OCD (reducing fear/anxiety vs. delusion/disorganized behavior). While it relates to the Disorganized_Abnormal_Behavior, the specific question about the internal motivation (reducing unwanted fear/anxiety vs preventing something definitely bad) is a differential diagnosis question (OCD vs Psychosis) that is not explicitly covered as a separate symptom profile item to answer with, but rather asks for clarification on the nature of the behavior.

patient.answer:
I don't really know if it was... anxiety, or what you'd call it. I don't know exactly what would happen, I just couldn't stop. It just felt completely wrong if they weren't in the right spots. The bags we use for the airway kits are this bright green color, you know? They match the oxygen tanks, the little D-cylinders we carry in the jump bag. It's so annoying when you have to swap those out and someone walked off with the oxygen wrench. We used to keep it on a little chain attached to the regulator, but the chain broke. Chains always break if the links are cheap. 

My brother has this massive, heavy-duty chain he uses to lock up his motorcycle. He's a mechanic, so he's really protective of his vehicles. He has this giant red Snap-on tool chest in his garage that probably costs more than my car. He actually painted his old Pontiac that exact same shade of red. We drove that thing all the way down to Florida one summer, and the AC went out right around Atlanta. It was brutal. We had to roll the windows down, and the wind noise on the highway is just deafening when you do that for hours. My left ear was ringing for two days after we got to the beach. The sand there gets everywhere, though. You can never really get it out of your shoes.

doctor.intent: Clarify whether the patient's belief that supervisors are watching him is a fixed delusion or an obsession with retained insight, to distinguish psychotic disorder from OCD.
doctor.question: Do you think there is any chance that the cameras are not actually being used to watch or target you?

target_item.name: Delusions
target_item.manifestation: I know the injury review people and some supervisors have been watching me through the station cameras and changing my triage notes to make me look unsafe, even when they tell me it's just routine paperwork.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if I think there is any chance the cameras are not actually being used to watch or target me, which directly relates to my delusions about being watched through the station cameras and having my triage notes changed.

patient.answer:
No, there's no chance. I know they're watching me. The injury review people, the supervisors, they're using those station cameras right now. I know they are. And they're going into the system and changing my triage notes, trying to make it look like I'm an unsafe medic. They can tell me all day long that it's "just routine paperwork," but I'm not stupid. I know what they're doing. 

It's just like when they tried to switch the charting software last year. They told us it was going to be faster, but the new tablets they bought were total garbage. The screens were so small, and the stylus they gave us would just snap if you pressed too hard. I broke three of them in one month. I hate those little plastic pens. I used to love drawing with charcoal when I was taking some art classes for my associate's degree. Charcoal is so messy, though, you get it all over your hands, and if you touch your face, you look like a chimney sweep. We had a call for a chimney fire once, back when I first started. The whole house smelled like burning pine for weeks. Pine is a nice smell, though, kind of like those little tree air fresheners people hang from their rearview mirrors. I always buy the vanilla ones, but they lose their scent after like two days. It's a total rip-off.

doctor.intent: Assess for a true thought disorder/disorganized thinking versus anxiety/OCD with poor insight by determining whether the patient has experienced hearing voices others cannot hear.
doctor.question: Have you been hearing voices when no one else is around?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about auditory hallucinations (hearing voices), which is not covered by any of the symptoms in my profile (Delusions, Disorganized/Abnormal Behavior, Negative Symptoms, Functional Impairment, Duration, Psychotic Symptoms Duration).

patient.answer:
Voices? No, I don't hear any voices. Just the normal stuff, you know, the radio chatter in my head sometimes after a long shift. We use these Motorola radios, and the static on the main dispatch channel is always so loud. You can turn the squelch down, but then you miss half of what central is saying. Central dispatch is located all the way downtown in this windowless basement. I had to go there once to pick up a new ID badge because the magnetic strip on mine stopped working. It wouldn't swipe to let me into the supply room anymore. 

The supply room is where they keep all the good trauma dressings, the big bulky ones. We go through those so fast on the weekends, especially when the bars close and people start fighting out on the street. I saw a guy get hit with a barstool once, completely shattered his jaw. They had to wire it shut for six weeks. I can't imagine having my jaw wired shut. You'd have to drink everything through a straw. I like milkshakes, but only if they're thick enough that you actually need a spoon. The diner near my apartment makes the best strawberry milkshakes. They use real strawberries, not that fake syrup stuff that tastes like cough medicine. I hate the taste of cherry cough syrup. It reminds me of being a kid and having strep throat. My mom used to try to hide it in orange juice, but you can always taste it. Orange juice is better with pulp anyway, it feels more real.

doctor.intent: Assess whether the patient has had a persistent depressed mood, which would help distinguish schizophrenia/schizoaffective disorder from OCD with poor insight
doctor.question: Over the past few weeks, have you been feeling down or depressed معظم of the day?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about depressed mood (feeling down or depressed most of the day), which is a symptom of depression. My symptom profile covers delusions, disorganized behavior, negative symptoms, functional impairment, and duration, but does not include depressive symptoms.

patient.answer:
Down? Depressed? I don't... no, I haven't really noticed feeling down most of the day. I mean, I get tired, sure. Working a 24-hour shift on the rig will do that to anyone. You're up all night running calls, and by the time morning rolls around, you feel like you've been run over by a truck. The suspension on our main ambulance is completely shot, too. Every pothole feels like you're hitting a brick wall. The city is supposed to be repaving the roads on the east side, but they've had the orange barrels out for six months and haven't done a thing. 

I hate driving through construction zones. The lanes get so narrow, and people never merge when they're supposed to. They always wait until the very last second and try to cut in front of you. My dad used to get terrible road rage when that happened. He drove this big Ford F-150, dark blue. He kept a CB radio in the cab so he could listen to the truckers. He loved listening to the truckers talk about the weigh stations and the speed traps. I always thought CB radios sounded so cool when I was a kid, with all the static and the weird codes they used. Ten-four, good buddy. It's kind of like our dispatch codes, but ours are a lot more boring. Just numbers and letters. Sometimes I wish we could use cooler call signs, like they do in the military. Like Maverick or Iceman. Top Gun is such a classic movie. The volleyball scene is iconic, but the soundtrack is really what makes it. I actually have the soundtrack on vinyl. Vinyl sounds so much warmer than digital, you know? It has that nice crackle when you put the needle down.

doctor.intent: Differentiate obsessive-compulsive disorder from psychotic disorders by assessing insight into the repetitive bag-moving ritual
doctor.question: Do you think the urge to keep arranging the airway bags is unreasonable or excessive?

target_item.name: Disorganized_Abnormal_Behavior
target_item.manifestation: They sent me here because at the station I kept moving the airway bags into a pattern I knew was right, repeating the dispatch numbers out loud, and I wouldn't step away when my lieutenant told me to stop because it felt like the whole bay would go bad if I broke the sequence.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the patient's urge to arrange airway bags, which directly corresponds to the manifestation of disorganized/abnormal behavior where the patient kept moving airway bags into a specific pattern.

patient.answer:
Unreasonable? No, it wasn't unreasonable at all, it was necessary. That's actually why they sent me here. At the station, I kept moving the airway bags into this pattern, a pattern I just knew was right. I had to do it. I was repeating the dispatch numbers out loud while I was arranging them, and my lieutenant kept telling me to stop and step away, but I wouldn't do it. I couldn't. It felt like the whole bay would go bad if I broke the sequence. Everything would just fall apart. 

My lieutenant, Miller, he just doesn't get it. He's always so tense anyway, probably because he drinks like four cups of that terrible gas station coffee every single shift. The stuff from those metal pump pots that sits there for hours and gets all scorched and bitter on the bottom. I don't know how anyone drinks that. If I go to the gas station on a shift, I usually just get a Gatorade. The light blue one, Glacier Freeze. It's really the only good flavor. The red one tastes like fruit punch, but like a weird, watered-down version of it. We used to make fruit punch in these massive orange coolers for the neighborhood block parties when I was growing up. Everyone on the street would bring a dish to share. Mrs. Gable next door always brought potato salad, but she put raisins in it. Who puts raisins in potato salad? It's completely wrong. Potatoes should be savory, you know, with mustard and a little bit of paprika on top. Paprika is a weird spice, though, because it doesn't really taste like much of anything, it just makes things red. Kind of like red dye number forty. I hate artificial food coloring, it always stains your tongue for the rest of the day.

doctor.intent: Clarify whether the fixed belief is a true bizarre delusion with thought insertion/passivity symptoms, which would favor schizophrenia-spectrum illness over OCD.
doctor.question: Do you ever feel like your thoughts are being put into your mind or controlled by someone else?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about thought insertion or thought control (delusions of control/thought insertion). The patient's symptom profile includes delusions (S019), but the manifestation specifically describes delusions of persecution/paranoia (believing injury review people and supervisors are watching through cameras and changing triage notes). It does not include thought insertion or control. Therefore, the profile does not cover this specific question.

patient.answer:
Controlled by someone else? No, no, they're my thoughts. Nobody is putting them in there. My head just gets really crowded sometimes, you know? Especially when we're running code three and the siren is just blaring right above the cab. We use those electronic sirens, the ones with the wail and the yelp settings. The yelp is supposed to be just for intersections to get people's attention, but some of the newer guys just leave it on yelp the whole way to the hospital. It's so piercing, it gives me a headache right behind my eyes. 

My partner, Dave, he always drives with his window cracked down, even in the dead of winter, just so he can hear the traffic better over the siren. Winter driving is the absolute worst in this city. The salt trucks never get to the side streets in time, and the rock salt just eats away at the undercarriage of the rigs anyway. You can see the rust creeping up the wheel wells by February. Rust is like a disease for cars. My first car was this old Honda Civic, and the floorboards were so rusted out I thought my foot was going to go straight through to the pavement like the Flintstones. The Flintstones always had those giant ribs that tipped the car over at the end of the credits. I always wondered what kind of animal those ribs came from. Brontosaurus, maybe? Dinosaurs are fascinating. When I was seven, I wanted to be a paleontologist. I had this whole collection of plastic dinosaurs, and I would bury them in my mom's garden and then dig them up with a little plastic shovel. She got so mad because I dug up all her tulip bulbs by accident. Tulips are nice, but they only bloom for like two weeks in the spring and then the petals just fall off everywhere and make a mess on the mulch. Mulch always smells so sour when it's fresh.

doctor.question: When you feel driven to repeat the numbers or arrange the bags, does it feel like the urge comes from your own mind and is unwanted?

target_item.name: Disorganized_Abnormal_Behavior
target_item.manifestation: They sent me here because at the station I kept moving the airway bags into a pattern I knew was right, repeating the dispatch numbers out loud, and I wouldn't step away when my lieutenant told me to stop because it felt like the whole bay would go bad if I broke the sequence.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the patient's urge to arrange the airway bags and repeat dispatch numbers, which directly relates to the manifestation of their disorganized/abnormal behavior.

patient.answer:
Unwanted? No, no, it's not unwanted. I have to do it. Like I said, that's the whole reason they made me come here. I was at the station, and I just had to keep moving the airway bags into this specific pattern. I knew it was the right pattern. And I was saying the dispatch numbers out loud while I did it, over and over. Miller, my lieutenant, he kept yelling at me to stop and step back, but I couldn't. If I broke the sequence, the whole bay was going to go bad. Everything would just be ruined. 

It's like when you're stocking the rig at the beginning of a shift. You have to make sure everything is in the exact right spot. The IV lines, the flushes, the gauze. If you reach for a tourniquet and it's not in the side pocket where it belongs, you're scrambling, and seconds matter. I hate those new CAT tourniquets they bought us, though. The windlass rod feels cheap, like it's going to snap if you crank it too hard. They switched suppliers a few months ago to save money. The city is always trying to save a buck on our gear, but then they go and spend millions on a new art installation downtown. It's this giant metal sculpture that looks like a crumpled up piece of tin foil. It's supposed to represent the flow of the river or something, but it's just blinding when the sun hits it. 

The sun has been so brutal lately, anyway. The AC in the back of our rig is barely blowing cool air. I tried to put in a maintenance request for it, but the mechanics are always backed up. They have this one mechanic, Gary, who works in the fleet garage. He always has grease under his fingernails. I don't think he ever really washes his hands. He eats these huge sub sandwiches for lunch while he's working on the engines, just getting mayo and oil all over the steering wheels. I can't stand mayonnaise. It's just eggs and oil whipped together, right? But it smells so sour if it sits out. My mom used to make egg salad sandwiches for school lunches, and by the time noon rolled around, my whole locker smelled like sulfur. Lockers in middle school were so small, I could barely fit my winter coat in mine. It was this puffy blue coat that made me look like a marshmallow. I hated that coat.

doctor.question: At any point, do you think the repeated bag-arranging and number-repeating is excessive or unreasonable?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the patient's insight into their bag-arranging and number-repeating behavior, which corresponds directly to the patient's disorganized/abnormal behavior.

patient.answer:
I feel like I just answered this. No, it wasn't excessive or unreasonable. Like I said, that's exactly why they sent me here in the first place. I was at the station, and I kept moving the airway bags into a pattern because I just knew it was right. I was repeating the dispatch numbers out loud, and my lieutenant kept telling me to stop and step away, but I wouldn't do it. I couldn't stop. It felt like the whole bay would go bad if I broke the sequence. 

The bay is always so echoey anyway, especially when the big roll-up doors are shut. They grease the tracks on those doors with this thick industrial lubricant that smells exactly like black licorice. I can't stand black licorice. My grandfather used to eat those little black jellybeans, the ones everyone else leaves at the bottom of the Easter basket. Easter grass is the worst invention ever, by the way. It's just shredded plastic that gets stuck in the vacuum cleaner brush. Our vacuum at the station is completely broken right now because the probie tried to vacuum up a bunch of spilled kitty litter. We keep kitty litter in the bay to soak up oil spills under the rigs. Oil is so hard to get off your boots. If you step in it, you leave these little black footprints all over the linoleum in the break room, and then the captain loses his mind. He's very particular about the floors. He actually makes us mop with this pine solution that makes my eyes water. Pine trees always remind me of those little air fresheners people hang from their rearview mirrors. They don't even smell like real trees, just chemicals.

doctor.question: When you think the injury review people are watching you through the cameras, could you be mistaken about that?

target_item.name: Delusions
target_item.manifestation: I know the injury review people and some supervisors have been watching me through the station cameras and changing my triage notes to make me look unsafe, even when they tell me it's just routine paperwork.
target_item.reason: The doctor is directly asking about the patient's belief that the injury review people are watching him through cameras and questioning whether he could be mistaken, which probes the fixity of his delusion.

patient.answer:
Mistaken? No, I'm not mistaken. I know the injury review people and some of the supervisors have been watching me through the station cameras. They keep changing my triage notes to make me look unsafe, even when they sit there and tell me it's just routine paperwork. They think I don't see it, but I know what I wrote. 

They use those little dome cameras in the corners of the ceiling, the ones with the smoked glass so you can't tell which way the lens is pointing. They installed those last year when they upgraded the security system. The guy who put them in left a bunch of drywall dust on the floor in the hallway, and nobody bothered to sweep it up for a week. Drywall dust is so fine, it just gets into everything. It's like baby powder, but gritty. My sister used to use baby powder all the time when my nephew was born. He had the worst diaper rash. She tried every cream on the market, but nothing worked until she switched to cloth diapers. Cloth diapers seem like so much work, though. You have to wash them constantly, and the washing machine at her house is this ancient top-loader that sounds like a jet engine taking off during the spin cycle. Jet engines are incredibly loud, obviously. We had to do a standby at the airport once for a plane that blew a tire on landing, and the noise out on the tarmac was deafening. Even with those big foam ear muffs, you could feel the vibration in your chest. Vibrations always make my teeth ache, right in the back where my wisdom teeth used to be. I had them out when I was nineteen, and the oral surgeon gave me laughing gas. It didn't make me laugh, it just made my arms feel like they were floating away like balloons. Balloons are terrible for the environment, especially the Mylar ones. They get tangled up in power lines and cause outages. We had a call last summer where a transformer blew because of a foil balloon, and this whole neighborhood lost power for two days right in the middle of a heatwave. Heatwaves are miserable when you're stuck wearing dark blue uniform pants that don't breathe at all.

doctor.intent: Assess whether there is a fixed delusional belief versus an ego-dystonic obsession, which best separates psychotic disorder from OCD.
doctor.question: Do you ever think these camera and note changes might be a false belief or a mistake on your part?

target_item.name: Delusions
target_item.manifestation: I know the injury review people and some supervisors have been watching me through the station cameras and changing my triage notes to make me look unsafe, even when they tell me it's just routine paperwork.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the patient has insight into their belief about the cameras and note changes, which directly relates to their delusions.

patient.answer:
I feel like we are going in circles here. I literally just told you it is not a mistake. It is not a false belief. I know for an absolute fact that the injury review people and the supervisors are watching me on the station cameras. They are going in and changing my triage notes because they want to make me look unsafe. And they can sit there and tell me it is just routine paperwork all they want, but I know what is really happening. 

Speaking of routine paperwork, they make us fill it out with these cheap blue pens. The ones where the caps always crack. My partner, Dave, he chews on his pen caps until they are just mangled pieces of plastic. It is completely disgusting. And when he is not chewing them, he clicks them. Click, click, click, the whole time we are sitting in the cab waiting for a dispatch. It drives me absolutely insane. It sounds exactly like the metronome my piano teacher used to use when I was a kid. Mrs. Higgins. She had this old wooden metronome that ticked so loud you could hear it out in her driveway. She lived in this massive Victorian house that always smelled like mothballs and peppermint. Peppermint is actually supposed to settle your stomach, you know. Whenever we get a patient in the back of the rig who is nauseous, I tell them to sniff an alcohol prep pad because it works just like peppermint. But a lot of people hate the smell of rubbing alcohol. They say it reminds them of hospitals. I don't really mind hospitals, but the lighting in the ER triage area is always so harsh. Those long fluorescent tubes give me a headache right behind my eyes. It is the exact same kind of headache you get when you eat ice cream too fast. Brain freeze. I actually haven't had ice cream in months. The soft serve machine at the dairy freeze down the street from the station has been broken since April. They claim it is a supply chain issue with the parts, but I am pretty sure the teenagers working there just don't want to clean it at night. Cleaning those machines takes forever because you have to take apart all those sticky little valves and O-rings.

doctor.intent: Assess whether the fixed beliefs occur only in the context of contamination/obsessional thoughts or are part of a broader psychotic syndrome
doctor.question: Do you ever have other beliefs that seem very clearly true to you but that other people say are impossible or not real?

target_item.name: Delusions
target_item.manifestation: I know the injury review people and some supervisors have been watching me through the station cameras and changing my triage notes to make me look unsafe, even when they tell me it's just routine paperwork.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if I have any other fixed beliefs that others consider impossible or not real, which is a direct inquiry about other potential delusions.

patient.answer:
I just... I don't understand why you keep asking me the same thing over and over. I literally just told you about this. The only thing I know for sure is what I've been saying this whole time—the injury review people and the supervisors, they are watching me on those station cameras. They are going into the system and changing my triage notes to make me look like an unsafe provider. They look me right in the eye and say it's just routine paperwork, but it's not. I know it's not. 

Paperwork is the bane of my existence anyway. We switched to this new electronic patient care reporting system last year, and the tablets they gave us are completely useless. The touch screens only work half the time, especially if you have gloves on. Nitrile gloves make your hands sweat so much in the summer. When you take them off, your hands look like you've been sitting in the bathtub for an hour. My mom used to make me take bubble baths when I was little, but she always bought this cheap off-brand bubble bath that smelled like fake strawberries. It didn't even make good bubbles, they would just pop after two seconds. You need the kind with glycerin to make the really big bubbles that last. Glycerin is actually a byproduct of making soap, I think. Or maybe it's biodiesel. Biodiesel smells like French fries when it burns. There's this guy in my neighborhood who converted an old Volkswagen Jetta to run on vegetable oil from the diner down the street. The diner has the best hash browns, they're always perfectly crispy on the edges. I like to put hot sauce on them, but only the green kind. The red kind has too much vinegar. Vinegar is great for cleaning windows, though. It doesn't leave streaks like the blue spray stuff does. The blue spray always leaves a film if you wipe it with paper towels instead of a microfiber cloth. Microfiber cloths are amazing because they pick up everything, but if you wash them with regular towels, they get covered in lint and they're basically ruined. Lint traps in dryers are huge fire hazards if you don't clean them out. We go to at least three dryer fires a year, usually in those big apartment complexes where people just shove their clothes in and walk away.

doctor.intent: Assess for compulsions/rituals characteristic of OCD rather than primary psychosis
doctor.question: Do you feel driven to repeat the bag-arranging or number-repeating to relieve a feeling of tension or anxiety?

target_item.name: Disorganized_Abnormal_Behavior
target_item.manifestation: They sent me here because at the station I kept moving the airway bags into a pattern I knew was right, repeating the dispatch numbers out loud, and I wouldn't step away when my lieutenant told me to stop because it felt like the whole bay would go bad if I broke the sequence.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the patient's specific behavior of arranging the airway bags and repeating dispatch numbers, which matches the manifestation for disorganized/abnormal behavior.

patient.answer:
Yeah, I mean, that's why they sent me here in the first place. At the station, I kept moving all the airway bags into this pattern that I just knew was right, and I was repeating the dispatch numbers out loud while I was doing it. My lieutenant kept telling me to stop and step away, but I wouldn't do it. I couldn't. It felt like the whole bay would go bad if I broke the sequence, so I had to keep going. 

But the bay... the floors in the ambulance bay are so dangerous anyway. They painted them with this gray epoxy last spring, but they didn't mix enough of the anti-slip grit into the paint. Grit is really important for traction, you know? It's just like when they salt the roads in the winter. The salt trucks always rust out so fast because the rock salt just eats right through the metal undercarriage. My dad had an old Chevy truck that rusted out completely around the wheel wells. He tried to patch it himself with fiberglass and Bondo, but Bondo smells so terrible when it's curing. It has this really sharp chemical odor that gets stuck in your nose. It's kind of like the smell of those heavy-duty bleach wipes we use to clean the stretcher mattresses. Those wipes dry out my hands so badly. I have to use this special lotion with colloidal oatmeal in it, but the smell of oatmeal always makes me think of those little packets of instant maple brown sugar oatmeal my mom made me before school. Maple syrup is impossible to clean up if you spill it. If you leave even a drop on the counter, it attracts ants instantly. Ants are incredibly organized, though. They follow those invisible pheromone trails for miles just to find one little crumb of sugar. Sugar is terrible for your teeth.

doctor.intent: Assess whether there has been a distinct period of elevated/expansive mood or increased energy, which would help distinguish bipolar/schizoaffective disorder from OCD with poor insight or schizophrenia.
doctor.question: Have you had any period when you felt unusually energized or euphoric for several days in a row?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about manic or hypomanic symptoms (feeling unusually energized or euphoric), which is not covered by any of the items in my symptom profile.

patient.answer: No, I don't really get like that. I mean, I have normal energy, I guess. I'm not bouncing off the walls or anything. Energized... well, energy drinks are really popular at the station. Everyone drinks those huge cans of Monster or Red Bull. Red Bull gives me the jitters, honestly. It has way too much taurine in it. Taurine is supposed to be an amino acid, but I read somewhere that they originally isolated it from bull bile, which is completely disgusting if you think about it. Bile is stored in the gallbladder, and we get so many calls for gallbladder attacks in the middle of the night. People eat a huge, greasy meal at like 9 PM, and then by 2 AM they are calling 911 because they think they are having a heart attack. Greasy food is the worst for you. The diner I was talking about before, the one with the good hash browns? They deep fry their onion rings in the same oil they use for the fish on Fridays, so the onion rings always taste a little bit like cod. Cod is a really flaky fish, but it doesn't have a lot of flavor on its own. You have to put a ton of tartar sauce on it. Tartar sauce is basically just mayonnaise and relish, and I absolutely hate mayonnaise. The texture is just wrong. It's like eating cold lotion. Lotion always makes my hands too slippery to put on my nitrile gloves, which is why I only use that oatmeal kind at night before I go to sleep. Sleep is so hard to get at the station anyway because the tones drop all night long. Even when it's not our rig getting dispatched, the lights come on and the speaker blares. It's impossible to get any real rest.

doctor.intent: Assess for obsessive-compulsive symptoms by determining whether he recognizes the bag-arranging behavior as unwanted/intrusive
doctor.question: When you had the urge to arrange the bags and repeat the numbers, did those thoughts feel intrusive or unwanted?

target_item.name: Disorganized_Abnormal_Behavior
target_item.manifestation: They sent me here because at the station I kept moving the airway bags into a pattern I knew was right, repeating the dispatch numbers out loud, and I wouldn't step away when my lieutenant told me to stop because it felt like the whole bay would go bad if I broke the sequence.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking a follow-up question about the patient's urge to arrange the airway bags and repeat numbers, which is a manifestation of their disorganized and abnormal behavior, to determine if these urges are intrusive or unwanted (like in OCD).

patient.answer:
I already said this. I literally just explained this to you. They didn't feel intrusive, they felt... necessary. Like I said, I was moving the airway bags into the pattern that I just *knew* was the right way they had to go, and I was repeating the dispatch numbers out loud. My lieutenant kept telling me to stop and step away, but I wouldn't do it. I couldn't stop. It felt like the whole bay would just go bad if I broke the sequence, so I had to keep going, and that's why they sent me here. 

But sequences are really important, especially in dispatch. If the dispatchers get the address sequence wrong, you end up on the complete opposite side of the county. The county is so huge, anyway. It takes forty-five minutes just to drive from the north end to the south end on the interstate. The interstate is always backed up on Friday afternoons because everyone is trying to go up to the lake for the weekend. People tow these massive boats with trucks that aren't rated for that kind of weight, and it completely ruins the transmission. Transmissions are so expensive to rebuild. My uncle had a transmission shop for twenty years, but he had to close it because he developed this terrible allergy to transmission fluid. It made his hands break out in these horrible red hives. Hives are basically an histamine reaction, right? You have to give Benadryl for that. Benadryl always makes people so sleepy. I took it once for a bee sting, and I slept for fourteen hours straight. I usually can't sleep for more than four hours at a time because of the tones at the station, like I was telling you. The station beds are terrible, too. They have these plastic covers on the mattresses so you can wipe them down, but they make you sweat so much. Sweating always makes me dehydrated, and then I get these terrible headaches right behind my eyes.

doctor.intent: Clarify whether the belief about cameras/note changes is a fixed delusion versus an obsession with preserved insight
doctor.question: When you think about the cameras and the triage notes, do you ever recognize that this might be a false belief?

target_item.name: Delusions
target_item.manifestation: I know the injury review people and some supervisors have been watching me through the station cameras and changing my triage notes to make me look unsafe, even when they tell me it's just routine paperwork.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the patient recognizes their beliefs about being watched through cameras and having their triage notes changed as potentially false, which directly addresses their delusions.

patient.answer:
No, it's not false. Why would it be false? I know they're doing it. The injury review people and some of the supervisors, they've been watching me through the station cameras. I know they are. And they're changing my triage notes, going in and altering the system to make me look unsafe. They keep telling me, "Oh, it's just routine paperwork, it's just a standard audit," but I know what they're actually doing. 

Paperwork is completely out of control in this field anyway. We used to do everything on paper trip tickets, with the carbon copies underneath. You had to press so hard with your pen to make sure it went through to the bottom yellow sheet. Yellow is such a terrible color. They painted the new fire engines yellow in the 90s because some study said it was more visible than red, but everyone hated it. It just doesn't look like a real fire engine if it's not red. Red is the color of stop signs, too. People run stop signs all the time in my neighborhood. They just roll right through them without even tapping the brakes. Brakes are so expensive to replace now, especially the rotors. You have to get them machined if they get warped, but most places just want to sell you brand new ones because they make more money on the parts. Parts for foreign cars take forever to ship. My buddy ordered a bumper for his Subaru and it sat on a cargo ship in the port of Los Angeles for three months. Los Angeles has terrible smog. I could never live somewhere where the air is brown.

opening_question.intent: Open the interview and elicit the patient’s chief concern.
opening_question.question: Hello, I’m glad you came in. What brings you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The interview shows persistent, distressing compulsive behaviors and associated intrusive-seeming urges centered on arranging airway bags into a precise pattern and repetitively saying dispatch numbers, with the patient feeling unable to stop and believing that stopping would lead to something bad happening to the bay. He consistently denies that these thoughts are delusions, hallucinations, or mood-related. Although he also has fixed persecutory beliefs about cameras and note changes, the core presentation is repetitive ritualized behavior driven by anxiety/need for completeness, making obsessive-compulsive disorder the best fit. Psychotic disorders remain in the differential because of the paranoia, but no clear hallucinations, formal thought disorder, or mood episode were established.
